subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 10 periods = 450 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 7h 30min

periods.stage_label: Observe and record: matter is made of particles
periods.activity_title: Chalk and Sugar: First Evidence for Particles
periods.activity_description: Students grind chalk to fine powder and dissolve sugar in water. They observe that chalk remains chalk at every scale and that sugar disappears visually yet its presence persists as taste, establishing that matter consists of extremely small constituent particles.

roles.role_description: Sets up the two activities, guides observation, and introduces the term constituent particle after students share their findings.
Grind chalk, stir sugar into water, record observations about what changes and what stays the same in each case.

time_bands.activity: Teacher frames the chapter's central question — what is matter made of — and students predict whether chalk can be broken indefinitely.
Groups grind chalk to powder, examine specks, then dissolve sugar in water and taste the solution; observations are recorded in notebooks.
Groups share findings; class discussion surfaces the key pattern: matter subdivides but each fragment is still the same substance, and dissolved particles are invisible yet present.
Teacher formally introduces the term constituent particle and connects both activities to the foundational claim that all matter is composed of enormous numbers of very small particles.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the chapter's opening unit, so orient students to the idea that today's hands-on work is building the core vocabulary of the entire chapter. Watch for the common conflation of 'particle disappears' with 'particle ceases to exist' when sugar dissolves — the taste test is the decisive counter-evidence to press on. A useful checkpoint: students are ready to move on when they can state, in their own words, that the sugar particle occupies the space between water molecules rather than vanishing.
materials: mortar and pestle or two stones

periods.stage_label: Observe and record: matter is made of particles
periods.activity_title: Invisible but Real: Interparticle Spaces in Liquids
periods.activity_description: Students mark the water level in a container, add sugar and allow it to dissolve completely, then re-read the volume. They observe that the solution volume is less than the sum of the two original volumes, and contrast this with what happens when insoluble sand is added instead.

roles.role_description: Poses the investigation question, circulates to prompt prediction before addition, and draws the contrast between sugar and sand outcomes in the closing discussion.
Mark initial water level, add sugar, wait for full dissolution, mark new level, and compare results with a group that added sand instead.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the question: if you add sugar to water, will the total volume equal water volume plus sugar volume? Students record predictions.
Groups carry out the sugar-dissolution version; a parallel set of groups add sand; all mark and compare before-and-after volumes carefully.
Groups report their volume readings; class compares sugar result with sand result and proposes explanations for why sugar decreases total volume while sand does not.
Teacher connects the sugar result to interparticle spaces — dissolved particles fit into the gaps between water molecules — reinforcing the particle model from the previous unit.

periods.teacher_notes: In the previous unit students established that constituent particles are real but invisible; this unit adds the structural idea that liquid particles have spaces between them. The most common error here is students attributing the volume reduction to sugar 'melting' rather than to particles fitting into interparticle spaces — probe this by asking why sand, which also dissolves in everyday language, does not show the same effect. Ensure each group records both the before and after levels with the container on a flat surface to minimise parallax reading errors.
materials: measuring cylinders or calibrated transparent containers

periods.stage_label: Classify by observable properties: the three states
periods.activity_title: Shape, Volume, and Compressibility: Sorting the Three States
periods.activity_description: Students handle a set of solid objects (iron nail, rock salt, stone, wood key, aluminium strip) and observe their fixed shape and volume, then transfer 200 mL of water across three differently shaped containers and compress air and water with a syringe, building a classification of the three states by observable properties.

roles.role_description: Prepares the object set, demonstrates the syringe compression safely, and guides students to frame their classifications as testable criteria rather than lists.
Examine and describe solid objects, perform the liquid transfer across containers, and operate the syringe for gas and water compression, recording observations systematically.

time_bands.activity: Groups examine the solid object set, recording shape and volume observations for each; teacher circulates asking whether any solid has taken the shape of their hand.
Groups transfer 200 mL of water between three differently shaped containers, confirming that volume is fixed while shape changes, and record the pattern.
Teacher demonstrates and then groups repeat syringe compression — first with air (compressible), then with water (incompressible) — and record the contrasting outcomes.
Class builds a shared classification table on the board: solid, liquid, gas; columns for fixed/variable shape, fixed/variable volume, compressibility.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous two units established that matter has particles; this unit shifts to classifying matter by what we can observe with our senses and simple instruments. A frequent confusion is that students describe liquids as having no definite shape but then incorrectly extend this to say liquids have no definite volume — pressing on the marked 200 mL across all three containers is the corrective. Ensure the syringe plunger is sealed at the nozzle end with a finger before compressing, so the difference between air and water is dramatic and unambiguous.

periods.stage_label: Classify by observable properties: the three states
periods.activity_title: Smoke, Spread, and Fluid Flow: Observing Gas and Liquid Behaviour
periods.activity_description: Students observe smoke from a burning incense stick collected in one gas jar, then watch it spread when a second inverted jar is placed on top, and separately observe the spread of fragrance from an incense stick burning in a corner, classifying gases and liquids together as fluids on the basis of their shared flow behaviour.

roles.role_description: Manages the incense stick safely, facilitates the gas jar transfer demonstration, and poses the question of what gases and liquids share that solids do not.
Observe and record the smoke transfer between gas jars and the spread of fragrance, then propose and justify a classification that groups liquids and gases together.

time_bands.activity: Teacher lights incense stick; smoke is collected in Gas Jar A and the class observes that smoke fills the jar; students predict what will happen when Jar B is inverted onto A.
Teacher performs the jar inversion; students observe smoke distributing between both jars and record: gas fills all available space and spreads without any push from outside.

Students recall from the previous unit that liquids also flow and take the shape of their container; small groups draft a justification for classifying both liquids and gases as fluids, contrasting with solids.
Groups share justifications; class converges on the fluid classification and adds it to the table from the previous unit; teacher formally introduces the term fluid.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit builds directly on the three-state classification table from the previous unit, adding fluid behaviour as a cross-cutting property. Watch for students claiming that gases have no mass — this misconception is not resolved in this chapter but can be neutralised by pointing out that smoke is visible and therefore detectable. A good probe: ask whether water flowing from a tap and smoke filling a room are similar events, and why solids never behave that way.
materials: two glass gas jars with lids or cardboard covers

periods.stage_label: Explain using the particulate model: interparticle forces and spacing
periods.activity_title: Why Particles Stay Together: Interparticle Attraction and Distance
periods.activity_description: Students are introduced to interparticle attraction as the force holding particles together and to the inverse relationship between interparticle distance and force strength. They examine the melting point data table for ice, urea, and iron and use it to rank substances by the strength of their interparticle forces.

roles.role_description: Presents the concept of interparticle attraction, explains how force strength changes with distance, and uses the melting point data to demonstrate how observable properties encode information about submicroscopic forces.
Analyse the melting point data table, rank the three substances by inferred interparticle attraction strength, and write a short justification for their ranking.

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains interparticle attraction: particles attract each other; this force is strongest when particles are close and weakens sharply even with a slight increase in distance; students take notes and ask clarifying questions.
Teacher presents the melting point data (ice 0°C, urea 133°C, iron 1538°C) and asks students to infer which substance has the strongest interparticle forces and why.

Students individually write a ranked explanation — ice, urea, iron from weakest to strongest — justifying the ranking using the idea that a higher melting point means more thermal energy is needed to break interparticle attractions.
Selected students share justifications; teacher corrects any reasoning that equates melting point with 'how solid something feels' rather than with the strength of interparticle forces.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous two units were entirely observational and classificatory; this unit introduces the submicroscopic explanation for the first time, so the conceptual gear-change is significant. The key misconception to address is that iron is hard because it is heavy — redirect students firmly to the idea that hardness and high melting point both trace back to strong interparticle attractions, not to the mass of the object. A useful check: a student is ready when they can say 'iron has a higher melting point than ice because its interparticle attractions are stronger, so more energy is needed to separate the particles.'

periods.stage_label: Explain using the particulate model: interparticle forces and spacing
periods.activity_title: Particle Motion in Liquids: Permanganate Spread and Temperature
periods.activity_description: Students drop a grain of potassium permanganate into water at three temperatures — hot, room temperature, and ice-cold — and observe how quickly the pink colour spreads, then propose an explanation linking the rate of spread to the energy and motion of liquid particles.

roles.role_description: Prepares the three water temperatures in advance, manages safe handling of hot water, and presses groups to connect the observation to the particle model rather than to a vague idea of 'water mixing'.
Drop one grain of permanganate into each temperature of water, observe and time the colour spread qualitatively, then construct a group explanation using particle motion and thermal energy.

time_bands.activity: Teacher shows the three water samples and asks students to predict in which temperature the pink colour will spread fastest and slowest; predictions are recorded.
Groups carry out the three trials simultaneously where possible, observing and sketching the spread pattern; qualitative timing (quick sketch at equal intervals) is recorded.
Groups draft explanations: more thermal energy means particles move faster, carrying the permanganate colour throughout the water more rapidly; groups compare explanations.
Class converges on the explanation; teacher connects this to the chapter's general principle that thermal energy governs particle motion across all states.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit extends the particulate explanation established in the previous unit from static attraction to dynamic motion — a crucial progression. The common error is students saying the hot water 'dissolves the colour faster', which attributes the effect to the water acting on the crystal rather than to particle motion carrying the colour; redirect by asking what is actually moving after the grain has fully dissolved. If potassium permanganate is unavailable, a drop of food colouring or ink at two temperatures gives a clear enough contrast for the same reasoning.
materials: tweezers or a toothpick for placing the grain

periods.stage_label: Explain using the particulate model: interparticle forces and spacing
periods.activity_title: Gas Particles in Motion: Fragrance, Freedom, and Negligible Forces
periods.activity_description: Students burn an incense stick in one corner of the room and track when and where the fragrance is first detected, then construct a particle-level explanation for why gas particles spread rapidly in all directions without needing a push, contrasting particle freedom in gases with the restricted motion in liquids.

roles.role_description: Manages the incense stick safely, directs students to stand in different positions in the room, and structures the contrast with the liquid permanganate activity from the previous unit.

Stand at assigned distances and directions from the incense stick, record when fragrance is detected, and individually write a particle-level explanation distinguishing gas particle motion from liquid particle motion.

time_bands.activity: Teacher lights incense stick in one corner; students are positioned at various distances and angles and asked to raise a hand the instant they detect the fragrance; teacher records the approximate detection pattern on the board.

Students individually write an explanation: gas particles move in all directions freely, interparticle attractions are negligible, and thermal energy is high enough that particles travel throughout the room rapidly.

Students compare their written explanations in pairs, then the class compares the gas fragrance result with the liquid permanganate result — which spread faster, and why does the particle model predict this?

Teacher formalises the contrast: in liquids, particles move but within limited space under weak attractions; in gases, attractions are negligible and motion is free in all directions, explaining rapid and complete spreading.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit completes the three-stage picture of particle motion by focusing on gases, complementing the liquid evidence from the previous unit. Students often think fragrance spreads because it is 'light' or because air currents carry it — challenge this by noting the chapter's language of random motion in all directions and asking whether air currents would explain detection at positions not in the direct airflow path. This is also the moment to reinforce that negligible interparticle attraction in gases is what makes them neither fixed-shape nor fixed-volume.

periods.stage_label: Apply the integrated model: thermal energy drives state changes
periods.activity_title: Melting, Boiling, and Evaporation: Thermal Energy Changes State
periods.activity_description: The teacher demonstrates heating ice to water to steam (or uses a candle wax melt as a simpler proxy) while narrating the particle-level changes at each transition. Students observe and annotate a particle diagram showing how particle arrangement, spacing, and motion change through melting and boiling, and distinguish evaporation from boiling using the chapter's definitions.

roles.role_description: Conducts the demonstration, pauses at each phase transition to ask students what is happening to particles, and introduces the formal definitions of melting point, boiling point, and evaporation.

Annotate a pre-drawn particle diagram at three states, labelling interparticle spacing, force strength, and type of particle motion at each stage, and write one sentence distinguishing boiling from evaporation.

time_bands.activity: Teacher heats ice (or wax) and pauses at the melting point: students annotate the solid-to-liquid transition on their diagram, noting particles leaving fixed positions and attractions weakening.

Teacher continues to the boiling point; students annotate the liquid-to-gas transition, noting particles gaining enough thermal energy to overcome attractions entirely, and bubble formation throughout the bulk.

Teacher explains evaporation as a surface-only, below-boiling-point process; students write one sentence distinguishing it from boiling and add an annotation to their diagram showing surface particle escape.
Pairs compare annotations and the class establishes consensus descriptions for each transition, which teacher records on the board as a reference summary.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous three units built the particle model in stages; this unit assembles those pieces into the complete state-change picture for the first time. The most persistent confusion here is between boiling and evaporation — students routinely think evaporation only happens when heat is applied; pressing on the chapter's statement that evaporation occurs at all temperatures and only at the surface is the key corrective. A useful probe: ask why a wet cloth dries overnight even in a cool room, and whether that is boiling.
materials: heat source (spirit lamp, hot plate, or candle)

periods.stage_label: Apply the integrated model: thermal energy drives state changes
periods.activity_title: Fig. 7.12 Unpacked: Building and Defending the Particle Summary
periods.activity_description: Students reconstruct the chapter's three-state comparison table — interparticle spacing, packing, attraction strength, and particle movement — from their own accumulated observations and explanations across previous units, then use the completed table to predict and explain particle-level events in two unfamiliar scenarios from the chapter's exercises.

roles.role_description: Presents the two unfamiliar scenarios from the chapter exercises, facilitates group reasoning, and challenges groups to justify every cell of their table with a specific observation from an earlier unit.
Collaboratively reconstruct the four-property comparison table from memory and earlier notes, then apply it to explain the two scenarios, producing a written group justification.

time_bands.activity: Groups reconstruct the comparison table without looking at the chapter, filling in interparticle spacing, packing density, attraction strength, and particle motion for solid, liquid, and gas; each group traces every cell back to a specific unit's observation.
Teacher presents two unfamiliar scenarios (drawn from the chapter's exercises): groups apply the table to explain what is happening at the particle level in each case and write their reasoning.
Groups present their scenario explanations; the class evaluates each explanation against the table — does the particle-level account correctly reflect spacing, force, and motion for that state?
Teacher clarifies any remaining gaps and confirms the completed table as the integrated summary of the chapter's particle model.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit is the most cognitively demanding of the chapter — students must apply the full integrated model rather than recall isolated facts. The typical weakness is that groups fill in the table correctly but then revert to observable-property language when explaining the scenarios, rather than genuinely using particle spacing, force, and motion; prompt with 'tell me what the particles are doing' each time a group says something like 'because gases are lighter'. Students who can defend every table cell with a prior observation are demonstrating exactly the final-stage operation this chapter targets.
homework: Choose one everyday phenomenon not covered in this chapter — such as a fragrance detectable across a room, or ice forming on a cold surface — and write a particle-level explanation using the interparticle spacing, force, and motion language from the summary table.

periods.stage_label: Apply the integrated model: thermal energy drives state changes
periods.activity_title: The Acharya Kanad Connection: Parmanu, Evidence, and Limits of the Model
periods.activity_description: Students revisit the 'Our Scientific Heritage' sidebar on Acharya Kanad's Parmanu concept and the 'A Step Further' note on SPM, then design a two-column argument — what the activities in this chapter provide as evidence for the particle model, and what remains unresolved or requires assumptions — producing a written evaluation of the model's explanatory power.

roles.role_description: Opens by reading the Parmanu sidebar aloud, frames the task as evaluating the chapter's own evidence, and circulates to ensure students distinguish empirical observations from model-level inferences.

Construct a two-column argument independently — evidence from activities that supports the particle model, and limitations or assumptions the model requires — and write a concluding sentence on the model's overall explanatory power.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the Parmanu sidebar aloud and briefly notes the SPM distinction; class discusses: what can we actually see, and what do we infer from what we see?

Students independently construct the two-column argument: left column lists specific activities (chalk grinding, sugar dissolution, syringe compression, permanganate spread, fragrance detection) with what each evidences; right column lists what is assumed or unresolved.
Students share concluding sentences; class discussion evaluates whether the activities together make the particle model convincing, and why no single activity is sufficient on its own.
Teacher closes by connecting the chapter's ten-unit arc: from the first question 'what is matter made of?' to the student's own evaluation of the model that answers it.

periods.teacher_notes: This closing unit asks students to step back and evaluate the very model they have been building — a higher-order operation that is appropriate here because it is the chapter's terminus. A common difficulty is students listing activities without stating what each one evidences; redirect by asking 'what specific claim about particles does grinding chalk support?' and distinguishing that from 'what did you observe?' The Acharya Kanad connection is not decorative — it positions the particle idea as a hypothesis that scientific activities test, which is the intellectual stance the whole chapter has been cultivating.
materials: chapter text (sections 'Our Scientific Heritage' and 'A Step Further')

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Observe and record: matter is made of particles
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students observe chalk grinding and sugar dissolution to establish that matter consists of extremely small constituent particles, and confirm interparticle spaces by measuring volume reduction when sugar dissolves in water.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can describe what chalk grinding and sugar dissolution reveal about the size and existence of constituent particles, and explain why solution volume is less than the sum of the component volumes.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Classify by observable properties: the three states
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students classify solids, liquids, and gases by observable properties — fixed/variable shape and volume, compressibility, flow — and justify grouping liquids and gases together as fluids.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can classify a given substance into solid, liquid, or gas by applying criteria of fixed shape, fixed volume, compressibility, and fluid behaviour, and justify the fluid classification with observed evidence.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Explain using the particulate model: interparticle forces and spacing
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students use interparticle attraction, interparticle spacing, and thermal energy to explain melting point data, the rate of permanganate spread at different temperatures, and the rapid random motion of gas particles detected as fragrance.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain differences in melting point, liquid particle motion rate, and gas particle spread by applying the concepts of interparticle attraction strength, interparticle spacing, and thermal energy.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Apply the integrated model: thermal energy drives state changes
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students annotate particle diagrams through melting and boiling transitions, reconstruct and apply the full three-state comparison table to unfamiliar scenarios, and evaluate the chapter's activities as evidence for the particulate model, reasoning simultaneously across classification properties and submicroscopic particle behaviour.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain the observable properties and state-changes of matter in unfamiliar scenarios by using the particulate model — constituent particles, interparticle attractions, interparticle spacing, and particle motion — to represent what is happening at the submicroscopic level in solids, liquids, and gases.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and record: matter is made of particles
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe what chalk grinding and sugar dissolution reveal about the size and existence of constituent particles, and explain why solution volume is less than the sum of the component volumes.

competency.competency_text: Classifying matter into three physical states by observable properties.

assessment_items.question_text: A student grinds a piece of chalk repeatedly until it becomes a very fine powder. Which statement best describes what has happened to the chalk?

options.label: A
options.text: Each speck of powder is still chalk; only the size of the pieces has changed.

options.label: B
options.text: The chalk has been converted into a different substance because its appearance has changed.

options.label: C
options.text: The chalk has dissolved into the air, as grinding is similar to dissolving.

options.label: D
options.text: The chalk particles have been destroyed because they are no longer visible to the naked eye.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Indicates a misconception that a change in appearance signals a change in substance identity — the student has not distinguished physical change from chemical change.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reveals the core target misconception of this stage: the student equates invisibility with non-existence, failing to grasp that constituent particles remain real even when too small to see.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Shows confusion between grinding (a mechanical physical change) and dissolving (particles entering interparticle spaces) — two distinct processes the chapter separates carefully.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the abstract concept of constituent particles can anchor their reasoning to the chalk-grinding activity: the powder still writes on a surface and still smells like chalk, which is direct sensory evidence that the substance has not changed.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and record: matter is made of particles
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe what chalk grinding and sugar dissolution reveal about the size and existence of constituent particles, and explain why solution volume is less than the sum of the component volumes.

competency.competency_text: Classifying matter into three physical states by observable properties.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Substance added to water | Volume of water before (mL) | Volume of solution/mixture after (mL)
Sugar (dissolves fully) | 100 | 118
Sand (insoluble) | 100 | 125
assessment_items.question_text: Refer to the table provided. Sugar and sand are each added to 100 mL of water. What does the comparison between the two results tell us about sugar particles?

options.label: A
options.text: Sand particles are larger than sugar particles, which is the only reason for the difference in volume.

options.label: B
options.text: Sugar makes water lighter, reducing the overall volume of the mixture.

options.label: C
options.text: Sugar particles are destroyed when they dissolve, which is why the volume increase is smaller.

options.label: D
options.text: Sugar particles occupy the spaces between water molecules, so they add less to the total volume than insoluble sand particles do.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Repeats the core misconception from the chalk activity — the student equates the invisible particle with a destroyed particle — now applied to dissolution.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Indicates a naïve density-based explanation: the student is attributing volume changes to weight rather than to interparticle spaces, showing no engagement with the particle model.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Shows partial reasoning — size difference is noticed — but the student has not connected size to the concept of interparticle spaces; they are explaining a correlation, not a mechanism.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who need a concrete anchor can be asked to imagine the sugar grains fitting into the gaps between tightly arranged marbles — a visualisation that connects directly to the activity's observable outcome without requiring prior abstract knowledge.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify by observable properties: the three states
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify a given substance into solid, liquid, or gas by applying criteria of fixed shape, fixed volume, compressibility, and fluid behaviour, and justify the fluid classification with observed evidence.

competency.competency_text: Classifying matter into three physical states by observable properties.

assessment_items.question_text: A student pushes the plunger of a sealed syringe filled with air and finds the air compresses easily. When the same syringe is filled with water, the plunger barely moves. Which pair of properties best explains this contrast?

options.label: A
options.text: Air has no definite volume and water has no definite shape, which causes the difference in behaviour.

options.label: B
options.text: Air is a fluid and water is not, so only air can be pushed.

options.label: C
options.text: Air is lighter than water, so the plunger can push it down more easily.

options.label: D
options.text: Air particles have large spaces between them, making it compressible; water particles are much more closely packed, making it practically incompressible.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Misapplies the fluid category — the student has confused 'fluid' (flows freely) with 'compressible'; this is a within-chapter conceptual confusion between fluid behaviour and compressibility.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Mixes up property assignments: water has a definite volume (a property the student observed directly), not an indefinite shape; this reveals imprecise retention of the classification table.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Substitutes density reasoning for particle-spacing reasoning — the student is drawing on everyday intuition about heaviness rather than the chapter's particle-spacing framework.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are not yet comfortable with particle language can articulate the answer in terms of 'spaces between particles' — the chapter's own phrasing — without needing to invoke formal terms like compressibility, and this is sufficient for this stage.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify by observable properties: the three states
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify a given substance into solid, liquid, or gas by applying criteria of fixed shape, fixed volume, compressibility, and fluid behaviour, and justify the fluid classification with observed evidence.

competency.competency_text: Classifying matter into three physical states by observable properties.

assessment_items.question_text: Smoke from an incense stick was collected in Gas Jar A. When Gas Jar B was inverted over Jar A, the smoke spread into both jars. Which property of gases does this observation directly demonstrate?

options.label: A
options.text: Gases have a fixed volume but take the shape of their container.

options.label: B
options.text: Gases fill all available space and have neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume.

options.label: C
options.text: Gases are fluids only when they are hot; cool gases behave more like solids.

options.label: D
options.text: Gases can be compressed because they move upward when released.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Assigns liquid properties to a gas — the student has confused the 'fixed volume, variable shape' description of liquids with the fully variable behaviour of gases.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Introduces a temperature-dependence misconception not supported by any chapter observation; the student may be confusing thermal expansion with the classification criterion of fluid behaviour.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Conflates compressibility with direction of movement — the student has linked two separate properties incoherently, suggesting the classification categories have not yet been internalised as distinct.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who connected the gas jar observation to the fragrance activity (incense stick in room corner) can use both observations together to justify their answer; either observation alone is sufficient evidence.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify by observable properties: the three states
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify a given substance into solid, liquid, or gas by applying criteria of fixed shape, fixed volume, compressibility, and fluid behaviour, and justify the fluid classification with observed evidence.

competency.competency_text: Classifying matter into three physical states by observable properties.

assessment_items.question_text: A student says: 'Liquids and gases are both fluids, so they must behave in exactly the same way.' Using observations from the chapter's activities, write two sentences explaining one way liquids and gases are similar and one way they are different.
expected_elements: Similarity: both liquids and gases flow and take the shape of their container, justifying the shared label 'fluid'.
Difference: liquids maintain a fixed volume while gases do not — a liquid transferred between containers keeps its volume, whereas gas expands to fill all available space.
At least one observation from a named chapter activity (e.g., water transfer across containers, smoke in gas jars) used to support the difference.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who are more comfortable with verbal than written responses can be asked to explain orally and then write one sentence; students who struggle with two properties simultaneously can be prompted to focus on the syringe experiment (compressibility) or the water-transfer experiment (fixed volume) as the anchor for their difference statement.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain using the particulate model: interparticle forces and spacing
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain differences in melting point, liquid particle motion rate, and gas particle spread by applying the concepts of interparticle attraction strength, interparticle spacing, and thermal energy.

competency.competency_text: Using the particulate model — constituent particles, interparticle attractions, interparticle spacing, and particle motion — to represent the properties of matter and explain state changes.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Substance | Melting Point (°C)
Ice | 0
Urea | 133
Iron | 1538
assessment_items.question_text: Refer to the table provided. Which conclusion about interparticle forces is best supported by the melting point data?

options.label: A
options.text: All three substances have the same interparticle forces but different amounts of heat are available in different environments.

options.label: B
options.text: Ice melts at the lowest temperature because its particles move faster than those of iron.

options.label: C
options.text: Iron has the strongest interparticle attractions, requiring the most thermal energy to allow particles to leave their fixed positions.

options.label: D
options.text: Iron melts at the highest temperature because its particles are the largest.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses particle size with interparticle attraction strength — a within-chapter conceptual error; the student is applying a macroscopic intuition (bigger objects are stronger) to a submicroscopic quantity.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Inverts the relationship between melting point and particle motion: the student believes lower melting point means faster intrinsic particle motion, rather than understanding that thermal energy input at the melting point is what drives the transition.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Denies the chapter's central explanatory move — that differences in melting point reflect differences in interparticle force strength — and replaces it with an environmental factor not supported by the chapter.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are not yet fluent in formal language can be asked to express the pattern in their own words: 'which substance needs more heat to melt, and what does that tell you about how tightly its particles hold on to each other?' This is the same reasoning in accessible language.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain using the particulate model: interparticle forces and spacing
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain differences in melting point, liquid particle motion rate, and gas particle spread by applying the concepts of interparticle attraction strength, interparticle spacing, and thermal energy.

competency.competency_text: Using the particulate model — constituent particles, interparticle attractions, interparticle spacing, and particle motion — to represent the properties of matter and explain state changes.

assessment_items.question_text: A grain of potassium permanganate is dropped into three beakers of water: one hot, one at room temperature, and one ice-cold. The pink colour spreads fastest in hot water. What does this observation reveal about the relationship between thermal energy and particle motion in liquids?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher thermal energy means liquid particles move faster, carrying the permanganate particles throughout the water more rapidly.

options.label: B
options.text: Hot water contains more permanganate colour because heat makes colours more visible.

options.label: C
options.text: Hot water has weaker interparticle forces, so there is more space for the permanganate to dissolve into.

options.label: D
options.text: The permanganate itself becomes a gas in hot water, which is why it spreads faster.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Attributes a perceptual change (colour visibility) to temperature rather than to particle motion — the student has not connected the spreading observation to particle dynamics at all.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses temperature effects on interparticle spacing with the chapter's specific point about interparticle motion; the student is partially using the model but misapplying it to spacing rather than motion speed.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Over-extends the gas state: the student knows gases spread faster but mistakenly attributes the enhanced spreading in hot water to a state change rather than to increased liquid particle motion speed.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are more confident with the gas fragrance activity than with the permanganate activity can be asked to reason by analogy: 'if gas particles spread faster because they move more freely, what would making liquid particles move faster do to the spread of permanganate?'

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain differences in melting point, liquid particle motion rate, and gas particle spread by applying the concepts of interparticle attraction strength, interparticle spacing, and thermal energy.

assessment_items.question_text: Fragrance from an incense stick burning in one corner of a room reaches students sitting in all other corners within a short time. Using the particulate model, explain why gas particles spread so rapidly in all directions, and why liquid particles spreading in water (as shown by the permanganate activity) are slower.
expected_elements: Gas particles have negligible interparticle attractions, so they are free to move in all directions without restriction.
High thermal energy in the gaseous state enables rapid, random motion throughout the room.
Liquid particles also move, but interparticle attractions are weak rather than negligible, restricting motion to within a limited space and making spreading slower.
The contrast is explicitly stated: gas spreading is faster because attractions are negligible and motion is free, whereas liquid spreading is slower because attractions still constrain motion.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find it difficult to write both explanations simultaneously can be encouraged to write the gas explanation first (anchored in the fragrance observation) and then contrast it with the permanganate result; the contrast can be as simple as 'in the liquid, particles still attract each other, so spreading is slower.'

assessment_items.question_text: When water is heated to its boiling point, bubbles form throughout the entire body of the liquid. At temperatures below the boiling point, the surface of the water slowly dries even without being heated strongly. Using the particulate model, which statement correctly distinguishes boiling from evaporation?

options.label: A
options.text: Boiling and evaporation are the same process; the only difference is the rate at which the liquid disappears.

options.label: B
options.text: Boiling occurs throughout the bulk when particles everywhere have enough thermal energy to overcome interparticle attractions; evaporation is a surface-only process occurring at all temperatures.

options.label: C
options.text: During boiling, surface particles escape into the air one by one; during evaporation, particles throughout the bulk gain enough energy to escape all at once.

options.label: D
options.text: Evaporation only happens when heat is supplied; boiling happens without any heat when the liquid is left exposed to air.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Reverses the two processes: the student has swapped the 'bulk' and 'surface' attributes, showing that the distinction has been encoded but the assignment to each process is inverted.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reflects the most common real-world misconception directly addressed in the chapter: the student believes evaporation requires applied heat, not understanding that it occurs at all temperatures when surface particles have sufficient individual energy.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Collapses a conceptually important distinction into a mere rate difference, failing to engage with the particle-level mechanism the chapter builds across multiple units.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who anchor the distinction in the wet-cloth example (cloth dries overnight without boiling) have a concrete real-world case that distinguishes the two processes without requiring formal language.

assessment_items.question_text: A student argues: 'Since both solids and liquids have interparticle attractions, they should both have fixed shapes.' Which response best uses the particulate model to evaluate this argument?

options.label: A
options.text: The argument fails because it ignores the difference in attraction strength: solid particles are held in fixed positions by very strong attractions, whereas liquid particles have weaker attractions that allow movement past each other, enabling liquids to flow and take the shape of their container.

options.label: B
options.text: The argument ignores temperature: at higher temperatures, solids also flow, making the distinction between solids and liquids only a matter of temperature and not of interparticle forces.

options.label: C
options.text: The argument is correct; liquids do have a fixed shape but it is hard to observe because they move too quickly.

options.label: D
options.text: The argument is wrong because liquids have no interparticle attractions at all, which is what allows them to flow.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Accepts the faulty argument, suggesting the student has not internalised the liquid classification criterion — variable shape — as a genuine observable fact distinct from solid behaviour.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Over-corrects: the student has remembered that liquids differ from solids but eliminates interparticle attractions in liquids entirely, contradicting the chapter's explicit statement that liquid attractions are weaker than solid, not absent.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Collapses state into a temperature continuum rather than recognising that each state has a characteristic particle arrangement — this reflects a failure to use the particulate model to distinguish states by mechanism rather than by thermal input alone.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who need a concrete anchor can be directed to the three-state comparison table they reconstructed: the 'attraction strength' row directly shows that solid attractions are very strong while liquid attractions are weak but present, which is the key distinction the question tests.

assessment_items.question_text: Iron is a solid at room temperature with a melting point of 1538°C. A student claims that the reason iron keeps its shape at room temperature and eventually melts at very high temperatures can be fully explained using just two ideas from the particulate model. Evaluate this claim: identify the two ideas the student might be using, explain how each one accounts for either the fixed shape or the eventual melting, and state whether two ideas are truly sufficient or whether a third is needed and why.
look_for: Identification of interparticle attraction as the idea that explains fixed shape: very strong attractions hold iron particles in fixed positions, preventing them from moving past each other.

Identification of thermal energy as the idea that explains melting: at 1538°C, thermal energy is sufficient to overcome the very strong interparticle attractions, allowing particles to abandon fixed positions.

A reasoned stance on sufficiency: either arguing that a third idea (interparticle spacing / particle vibration in the solid state) adds explanatory depth — particles vibrate about fixed positions below the melting point, which is why iron remains solid even though it is not completely static — or clearly justifying why two ideas are sufficient for the basic account.
Correct use of the chapter's language: 'fixed positions', 'thermal energy overcomes attractions', 'interparticle attractions', 'melting point' — used appropriately rather than as disconnected terms.
A clear distinction between the behaviour below the melting point (vibration without displacement) and at the melting point (displacement and flow).

ECR.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the evaluation stance ('are two ideas sufficient?') can be encouraged to answer the descriptive part first — what do the two ideas explain — and then simply state whether they feel something is missing; a partial evaluation that correctly identifies both ideas and explains each is a meaningful demonstration of the stage LO even without the meta-level judgment.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
State of matter | Observable property: shape | Observable property: volume | Observable property: compressibility | Particle-level explanation: interparticle spacing | Particle-level explanation: attraction strength | Particle-level explanation: type of particle motion | Which activity in this chapter provides the best evidence for your particle-level explanation?

assessment_items.task: Refer to the table provided. The left columns list observable properties of the three states; the right columns ask for particle-level explanations and the activity that best evidences each explanation. Complete the table and then write a short paragraph (three to four sentences) answering this question: Can the observable properties of a state of matter be fully predicted from its particle-level description alone? Use your completed table as evidence for your answer.
assessment_items.scaffold: For each state: (1) fill in the interparticle spacing column using minimum / moderate / maximum; (2) fill in the attraction strength column using very strong / weak / negligible; (3) describe the type of particle motion in one phrase; (4) name the specific chapter activity that most directly supports your particle-level claim. In your paragraph, pick one state and show how its three particle-level descriptors together predict all three of its observable properties — then state whether this means the model is fully sufficient or whether it leaves any observable property unexplained.
format_of_output: Completed six-column table (three states × three particle-level columns plus activity column)
A paragraph of three to four sentences evaluating the model's predictive power, with reference to at least one specific state and one specific activity from the chapter.

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Classification or sorting task with justification
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The final stage LO requires students to reason simultaneously across observable properties (the C-1.1 strand) and submicroscopic particle behaviour (the C-1.2 strand); a classification table with justification is the most natural demonstration vehicle because it makes both strands visible in a single structured output and requires explicit mapping between them.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response evidences the student's ability to hold the macroscopic classification (observable properties by state) and the submicroscopic model (particle spacing, force, motion) in simultaneous view and to evaluate whether the model's descriptors are sufficient to predict every observable property — integrating both co-central competencies in one act of reasoning.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The four-column structure separates observable facts from model claims and from evidential grounding; a student who can fill all three particle-level columns correctly and name a distinct activity for each state has demonstrated command of the whole model. The paragraph is where the evaluative move occurs — look for whether the student genuinely tests the model's predictive sufficiency rather than merely restating what they filled in the table.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses: correct and specific particle-level language in all three columns; distinct and appropriate activity citations for each state; a paragraph that identifies at least one observable property and traces it to particle-level cause; an honest engagement with whether any observable property (e.g., compressibility of gases) requires all three particle-level descriptors or just one. Weak responses: table filled with vague or recycled terms ('particles are far apart' applied identically to all states); activity column left blank or citing the same activity for all states; paragraph that restates the table without connecting macroscopic to submicroscopic or without any evaluative judgment on model sufficiency.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find the paragraph evaluative stance challenging can be invited to answer a simpler version: 'Pick one state. Can you predict all three observable properties from the particle description you wrote? Show how.' This partial evaluation still demonstrates integration of both competency strands and is a meaningful expression of the stage LO. Students who are more comfortable with diagrams than tables can annotate a simple particle diagram for each state instead of filling columns, and then write their paragraph from that.
